Stretch a wire or rubber band, sealed from heat — what does the thermometer do?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: Stretching a sample reversibly inside an insulating sleeve

Source

Concept
Reversible stretching at fixed entropy (the adiabatic stretching of a rod) and the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂f)T = (∂L/∂T)f, which gives (∂T/∂f)S = −(T/Cf)(∂L/∂T)f.
Serves
Explain how the sign of (∂L/∂T)f at the working tension decides the temperature change of a sample stretched reversibly with no heat exchange.
Inquiry
Six questions, each checked in the sim, then a closing summary card: stretch and release a steel wire, stretch a rubber band, let it reach room temperature while held, release it, and stretch it just past slack. The last question, where a barely stretched band cools like steel below about 0.36 N (the thermoelastic inversion), goes beyond the notes (Fermi Notes, §3.2, Eq. 3.46), which treat only the sign of (∂L/∂T)f for a taut band.
Misconception
Addressed only through the answer choices and their feedback. The sim reports the work done by the winch (W) and the temperature change (ΔT) side by side so the two can be compared directly.
Measured
ΔT = T − 293.15 K from the bead at mid-sample; ΔL = L − Lslack, with Lslack the slack length at 293.15 K; W = ∫ f dL since the last reset. Temperature is integrated in f by fourth-order Runge–Kutta with steps ≤ 1/2000 of the tension range; Cf = mc is held constant. Steel: E = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa, α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, 1.000 m × 1.00 mm. Rubber: ideal network f = bT(λ − λ⁻²), slack length 100.0 mm growing with β = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. The winch follows the slider at one third of the tension range per second; the heat exchange with the sleeve open is time-lapsed to about 2 s.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkSix question cards; each control appears only when a card first uses it, and each choice has its own feedback.
Operational quantitiesf in N, ΔL in mm, ΔT in mK and W in mJ, all computed live from the model.
Readout disciplineAt most two readouts during each card, in the Readouts panel of the sidebar; all four in free exploration. A typed box beside the tension slider sets exact values such as 0.30 N.
Stable axesEach sample has fixed chart axes that switch with the sample and never rescale.
Honest scalingThe band is drawn to scale with a 100 mm bar; the wire's extension is magnified and labelled; the heat exchange is labelled time-lapsed.
Loud state changesThe sleeve is drawn lifted aside with a SLEEVE OPEN tag; heat exchange appears on the chart as a dashed grey segment.
Instrument viewA dial thermometer wired to the bead reads the temperature the way the experimenter would.
Stretching a Wire and a Rubber Band
Apparatus (left) and temperature change against tension (right)

Guided Inquiry

1 · Stretching steel

With the steel wire slack at room temperature, raise the tension slowly to 200 N. What happens to the temperature of the wire?

2 · Releasing steel

Keeping the sleeve closed, lower the tension on the wire slowly from 200 N back to zero. What does its temperature do?

3 · Stretching rubber

Switch to the rubber band, slack at room temperature, and raise the tension slowly to 8 N. What happens to the temperature of the band?

4 · Letting the band cool

Hold the warm band at 8 N and press "Let it reach room temperature", watching the extension readout. What does the length of the band do as it cools?

5 · Releasing rubber

Now, with the band at room temperature under 8 N and the sleeve closed again, lower the tension slowly to zero. What does the temperature of the band do?

6 · Barely stretched rubber

Press ↺ Reset sample to slack, so the band is slack at room temperature, and raise the tension slowly to 0.30 N (type it in the box beside the slider), watching the temperature readout. What does the thermometer do?

7 · The sign of (∂L/∂T)f decides

Stretched reversibly with no heat exchanged, a sample keeps its entropy, so (∂T/∂f)S = −(T/Cf)(∂L/∂T)f.

Steel lengthens when warmed, so it cools as it is stretched. A taut rubber band shortens when warmed, so it warms, by several kelvin at 8 N; barely stretched, it behaves like steel until about 0.36 N.

The work done by the winch does not set the sign of ΔT; the sign of (∂L/∂T)f does. Press Finish to explore freely.

Stretching a Wire and a Rubber Band

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A steel wire or a rubber band hangs inside a closed insulating sleeve and a winch pulls it slowly. You read the tension, the extension, the work done by the winch and the change in temperature of the sample.

What you'll learn

  • Why a slow stretch inside a closed sleeve keeps the entropy of the sample fixed.
  • How the work done by the winch is counted.
  • How the Maxwell relation of Section 3.2 describes a stretched rod.
  • How the temperature change depends on the material and on the tension.
The set-up: a sample in a closed sleeve, a winch pulling with tension f, and a thermometer bead wired to a dial.

What's on screen

  • Scene (left): the sample on its clamp, the winch below it, and the dial wired to the thermometer bead.
  • Chart (right): ΔT against f, with fixed axes for each sample. Heat let out with the sleeve open appears as a dashed grey segment.
  • Readouts: f, the extension ΔL, ΔT = T − 293.15 K and the work W done by the winch.
See itReset the current sample to slack at room temperature, with the sleeve closed. Watch for: the dial at room temperature and every readout at zero.

03

The sleeve and a slow pull keep the entropy fixed

With the sleeve closed, no heat enters or leaves the sample. The winch follows the slider slowly, so the stretch is reversible. Together these conditions mean that the entropy S of the sample does not change.

The winch pulls with tension f through a small extension dL, so it does work f dL on the sample, and the combined law of the notes (§3.2) reads dU = T dS + f dL. The readout W adds this work up from slack:

Counted from the last reset of the sample.

While the sample is pulled out, f and dL are both positive, so W is positive for both samples. The sim shows W beside the temperature change ΔT = T − 293.15 K, read from a bead at the middle of the sample.

See itPull the steel wire to 200 N with the sleeve closed. Watch for: the work W, 127.0 mJ, counted from slack.
04

At fixed entropy, ΔT follows (∂L/∂T)f

The Legendre transform Φ = U − TS − fL has dΦ = −S dT − L df (3.43). Equal mixed second derivatives of Φ give the Maxwell relation

Notes (3.44).

Setting dS = 0 in dS = (∂S/∂T)f dT + (∂S/∂f)T df (3.45), and using (3.44), gives

Notes (3.46). Cf = T(∂S/∂T)f is the heat capacity at fixed tension.

A sample that lengthens when warmed at fixed tension cools when stretched, and one that shortens warms. Along this path T depends on f alone, so releasing the sample to f = 0 with no heat exchange returns T to its starting value.

See itStretch the current sample to a tension of your choice, or half its range from slack. Watch for: ΔT in the Readouts equal to the number in the panel above.
05

A stretched steel wire cools

The sim’s wire has α = 1.2 × 10−5 K−1 and E = 2.0 × 1011 Pa. It lengthens when warmed, so (∂L/∂T)f = αL0(1 + f/EA) is positive, and (3.46) makes ΔT negative.

Since f/EA is below 0.2% over the whole range, ΔT ≈ −TαL0f/Cf, with Cf = 2.84 J/K. It falls along a nearly straight line, to −248.1 mK at 200 N.

Steel, sleeve closed, from slack at 293.15 K. The dot is 200 N.

At 200 N the extension is 1.270 mm and the winch has done 127.0 mJ of work on the wire. The wire is colder all the same: the sign of ΔT comes from (∂L/∂T)f, not from the sign of W. Released slowly to zero, the wire returns to 293.15 K.

See itPull the steel wire to 200 N with the sleeve closed. Watch for: ΔT = −248.1 mK, ΔL = 1.270 mm and W = 127.0 mJ.
06

A taut rubber band warms when stretched and cools when released

The band is an ideal network, f = bT(λ − λ−2), with λ the stretch ratio. At fixed f a warmer band needs a smaller λ, so it shortens when warmed. At 8 N, (∂L/∂T)f = −1.24 × 10−3 m/K, against +1.2 × 10−5 m/K for the wire, so (3.46) makes ΔT positive.

Rubber, sleeve closed, up to 8 N. The dip of the first fraction of a newton is too small to see here.

With Cf = 0.361 J/K, ΔT = +3517.5 mK at 8 N, where the extension is 301.8 mm and W = 1371 mJ.

Hold 8 N and open the sleeve: the band cools to 293.15 K and lengthens by 4.29 mm. Close the sleeve and lower f to zero: ∂T/∂f is now positive, so T falls, and the band ends 3572.8 mK below room temperature.

See itPull the rubber band to 8 N with the sleeve closed. Then press Let it reach room temperature. Watch for: ΔT = +3517.5 mK at 8 N, and then ΔL growing by about 4 mm as the band cools.
07

A barely stretched band cools like steel

The slack length of the band grows with temperature, Ls = Ls0[1 + β(T − TR)] with β = 2.2 × 10−4 K−1, as a metal does. The network pulls the other way. At low tension the growth wins: (∂L/∂T)f is positive below 0.365 N, a stretch of about 6.5%, and negative above it.

The first 0.8 N of the band, from slack. ΔT bottoms out where (∂L/∂T)f changes sign.

So ΔT first falls, to −3.39 mK at 0.365 N, then rises and crosses zero at 0.704 N. At 0.30 N it is −3.3 mK, and at 0.50 N still −2.9 mK. At 0.80 N it is +2.3 mK.

See itPull the rubber band to 0.30 N with the sleeve closed. Watch for: ΔT = −3.3 mK, a fall, not the rise seen at 8 N.
08

Where it matters

  • Thermoelastic stress analysis. Infrared cameras record the millikelvin temperature changes of a metal part under cyclic load, and these map the stress in it. The sim’s wire at 200 N changes by 248 mK.
  • The rubber-band demonstration. A band stretched quickly and touched to the lip feels warm, and one released after it has cooled feels cold.
  • Elastocaloric cooling. Stretching, letting the heat out and releasing is a refrigeration cycle. Research devices use shape-memory alloys, whose temperature change on release is large.
09

Summary

In one line. A sample stretched slowly inside a closed sleeve keeps its entropy fixed, and this sim lets you stretch a steel wire or a rubber band and read the work, the extension and the temperature.

Key points

  • At fixed entropy, (∂T/∂f)S = −(T/Cf)(∂L/∂T)f.
  • Steel at 200 N: −248.1 mK. Rubber at 8 N: +3517.5 mK.
  • W = ∫f dL is positive for both samples and does not set the sign of ΔT.
  • Below 0.365 N the band behaves like the wire.

Common mix-ups

  • “Work done on a sample always warms it.” With no heat exchange, the sign of ΔT is the opposite of the sign of (∂L/∂T)f.
  • “Rubber obeys a different law from metal.” Both follow (3.46). Only the sign of (∂L/∂T)f differs.
  • “Warm the band by stretching, cool it, release it, and it is back where it started.” It ends 3572.8 mK below room temperature.

Things to try on your own

  • Pull the steel wire to 100 N and to 200 N, and compare the two values of ΔT.
  • Hold the band at 8 N, press Let it reach room temperature, then lower the tension to zero and read ΔT.
  • Type 0.30 N, 0.50 N and 0.80 N for the band and note the sign of ΔT each time.
